title.rhyme: Chapter 2: Zhang Fei in fury whips the Postal Knave; Royal Uncle He plots the eunuchs' grave.
title.prose: Chapter 2: Zhang Yide wrathfully whips the Postal Inspector; the Royal Uncle He plots to slay the eunuch lackeys.
title.original: 第二回：張翼德怒鞭督郵，何國舅謀誅宦豎

paragraphs.original: 且說董卓字仲顈，隴西臨洮人也。官拜河東太守，自來驕傲。當日怠慢了玄德，張飛性發，便欲殺之。玄德與關公急止之曰：「他是朝廷命官，豈可擅殺？」飛曰：「若不殺這廝，反要在他部下聽令，其實不甘！二兄要便住在此，我自投別處去也！」玄德曰：「我三人義同生死，豈可相離？不若都投別處去便了。」飛曰：「若如此，稍解吾恨。」
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Dong Zhuo, whose courtesy name was Zhongjiong; he was a man of Lintao in Longxi. He held the office of Grand Administrator of Hedong, and had ever been haughty by nature. On that day, having slighted Xuande, he provoked Zhang Fei's temper, and Fei would have killed him outright. Xuande and Lord Guan hastily checked him: "He is an officer appointed by the court—how can you kill him at your own will?" Fei said: "If I do not kill this wretch, I shall instead be obliged to take orders under his command, and that I cannot bear! If my two brothers wish to remain here, I shall go elsewhere alone!" Xuande said: "We three have sworn brotherhood in life and death; how can we part? Better that we all go together elsewhere." Fei said: "If it be so, my anger is in some measure eased."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), of style Zhongjiong, was born and bred
In Lintao town, where Longxi's plains are spread.
He ruled Hedong by court's commanding hand;
By nature haughty, proud throughout the land.
That day [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) had treated ill;
[Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) in fury rose, prepared to kill.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) and [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) cried: "A court-set lord!
Thou shalt not slay him with thy private sword!"
Said [Fei](char-zhang-fei): "If I let live this man of pride,
And take his orders, I cannot abide!
If ye, my brothers, here will choose to stay,
Then I alone shall seek another way."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied: "In oath we three are bound,
In life and death, our brotherhood is sound.
Why should we sunder? Far were better all
To other regions go, at duty's call."
Said [Fei](char-zhang-fei): "If thus we go, my wrath's allayed."
The three resolved, and forth their journey made.

paragraphs.original: 於是三人連夜引軍來投朱雋。雋待之其厚，合兵一處，進討張寶。是時曹操自跟皇甫嵩討張梁，大戰於曲陽。這裏朱雋進攻張寶。張寶引賊眾八九萬，屯於山後。雋令玄德為其先鋒，與賊對敵。張寶遣副將高昇出馬搦戰。玄德使張飛擊之。飛縱馬挺矛，與昇交戰，不數合，刺昇落馬。玄德麾軍直衝過去。張寶就馬上披髮仗劍，作起妖法。只見風雷大作，一股黑氣，從天而降：黑氣中似有無限人馬殺來。玄德連忙回軍，軍中大亂，敗陣而歸，與朱雋計議。雋曰：「彼用妖術，我來日可宰豬羊狗血，令軍士伏於山頭；候賊趕來，從高坡上潑之，其法可解。」
paragraphs.prose: So the three by night led their men to join with Zhu Jun. Jun received them with great kindness, and uniting their forces, advanced to suppress Zhang Bao. At that time Cao Cao followed Huangfu Song in pursuit of Zhang Liang, and fought a great battle at Quyang. Here Zhu Jun pressed his attack upon Zhang Bao. Zhang Bao led some eighty or ninety thousand rebels, and encamped behind a mountain. Jun appointed Xuande as the vanguard, to face the rebels in arms. Zhang Bao sent his deputy general Gao Sheng forth to give challenge, and Xuande sent Zhang Fei against him. Fei spurred his horse and brandished his spear; before few rounds were fought, he pierced Sheng and toppled him from his saddle. Xuande then waved on his troops and charged straight through. But Zhang Bao, mounted, let down his hair, took up his sword, and worked a demon-spell: there arose at once a great wind and thunder, and a column of black vapor descended from heaven; in the vapor there seemed to be horsemen without number, rushing forth to slay. Xuande in haste turned back his men; his army fell into great disorder, and they retreated in defeat. Xuande took counsel with Zhu Jun. Jun said: "He uses sorcery; tomorrow let us slaughter pigs, sheep, and dogs for their blood, and have the soldiers lie in wait upon the hilltop. When the rebels pursue, pour the blood down from on high; thus may his magic be broken."

paragraphs.original: 玄德聽令，撥關公、張飛各引軍一千，伏於山後高岡之上，盛豬羊狗血並穢物準備。次日，張寶搖旗擂鼓，引軍搦戰，玄德出迎。交鋒之際，張寶作法，風雷大作，飛砂走石，黑氣漫天，滾滾人馬，自天而下。玄德撥馬便走，張寶驅兵趕來。將過山頭，關、張伏軍放起號砲，將穢物齊潑。但見空中紙人草馬，紛紛墜地；風雷頓息，砂石不飛。張寶見解了法，急欲退軍。左關公，右張飛，兩軍都出，背後玄德、朱雋一齊趕上，賊兵大敗。玄德望見地公將軍旗號，飛馬趕來，張寶落荒而走。玄德發箭，中其左臂。張寶帶箭逃脫，走入陽城，堅守不出。朱雋引兵圍住陽城攻打，一面差人打探皇甫嵩消息。
paragraphs.prose: Xuande heeded the counsel, and detached Lord Guan and Zhang Fei, each with a thousand men, to lie in ambush upon a high mound behind the mountain, with pig, sheep, and dog's blood, and other unclean things, ready in store. The next day, Zhang Bao waved his banners and beat his drums, leading his forces out to challenge; Xuande rode forth to meet him. Just as they engaged, Zhang Bao again worked his magic: wind and thunder roared together, sand and stones flew about, the air was thick with black vapor, and a tide of horsemen tumbled down from heaven. Xuande wheeled his horse and fled; Zhang Bao pressed in pursuit. Just as they crossed the hilltop, the hidden troops of Guan and Zhang fired their signal-cannons and poured down the foul blood. There were seen paper men and grass horses falling from the sky; the wind and thunder at once ceased, and the sand and stones flew no more. When Zhang Bao saw his magic was broken, he turned to retreat in haste. From the left came Lord Guan, from the right Zhang Fei, both armies bursting forth at once; behind, Xuande and Zhu Jun gave chase together. The rebels were utterly defeated. Xuande, spying the General-of-the-Earth's banner, sped his horse in pursuit, and Zhang Bao fled into the wild. Xuande shot an arrow, which struck Bao through the left arm. Bao, with the arrow still in him, escaped and withdrew into Yangcheng, where he held firm and would not come out. Zhu Jun thereupon led his troops to encircle and attack Yangcheng, and at the same time dispatched men to inquire after the news of Huangfu Song.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) the counsel heard, and forthwith sent
Each, [Guan](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang](char-zhang-fei), with thousand men, intent;
On hilltop hid, behind the mountain laid,
With pig and sheep and dog's blood, all arrayed.
Next day [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao) with banners high uprear'd
Led forth his host; [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) in arms appear'd.
As battle joined, [Bao](char-zhang-bao) worked his sorcery:
Wind roared, and thunder; sand and stone flew free;
Black vapor wrapped the sky in dreadful gloom,
And horsemen poured from heaven, hosts of doom.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) wheel'd horse and turn'd at once in flight;
[Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao) pursu'd, with troops in pressing might.
Just as they crossed the hill, with sudden roar
[Guan Yu](char-guan-yu), [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) their signal-cannon bore;
And pour'd the blood and filth, profusely shed,
Upon the rebel host that hither sped.
Then paper men and grass-horse downward fell;
The wind, the thunder, ceased their fearful spell.
The flying sand and stones no longer rose;
And all the sorcery sank to peaceful close.
[Bao](char-zhang-bao) saw his arts undone, in haste to flee;
[Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) sprang left, and [Fei](char-zhang-fei) from right struck free.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) from the rear apace,
And cut the rebel host with bloody chase.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) beheld the 'Lord of Earth' on high;
Spurred horse, and chased [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao) with eager cry.
[Bao](char-zhang-bao) fled the field across the trackless plain;
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) drew bow — the arrow flew amain,
And smote his left arm; pierced, yet still he went,
To Yangcheng's gates his wounded pace was bent.
[Bao](char-zhang-bao) reached Yangcheng, and held the city tight,
Refusing battle though the foe drew nigh.
[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) encircled all in firm attack,
And sent to learn where [Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) might track.

paragraphs.original: 探子回報，具說：「皇甫嵩大獲勝捷，朝廷以董卓屢敗，命嵩代之。嵩到時，張角已死；張梁統其眾，與我軍相拒，被皇甫嵩連勝七陣，斬張梁於曲陽。發張角之棺，戮屍梟首，送往京師。餘眾俱降。朝廷加皇甫嵩為車騎將軍，領冀州牧。皇甫嵩又表奏盧植有功無罪，朝廷復盧植原官。曹操亦以有功，除濟南相，即日將班師赴任。」朱雋聽說，催促軍馬，悉力攻打陽城。賊勢危急，賊將嚴政，刺殺張寶，獻首投降。朱雋遂平數郡，上表獻捷。
paragraphs.prose: The scouts returned and made full report: "Huangfu Song has won a great victory. The court, because Dong Zhuo had been repeatedly defeated, has ordered Song to replace him. When Song arrived, Zhang Jiao was already dead; Zhang Liang had taken the leadership of the rebels and opposed our army, but in seven successive battles Song bore him down, and beheaded Liang at Quyang. They opened Zhang Jiao's coffin, mutilated the corpse, struck off the head, and sent it to the capital. The remaining rebels all surrendered. The court has promoted Huangfu Song to be General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Governor of Ji Province. Song further memorialized that Lu Zhi had merit and was guiltless; the court has restored Lu Zhi to his former office. Cao Cao, too, for his merit, has been appointed Chancellor of Jinan, and is to set out forthwith to take up his post." Zhu Jun, hearing this, urged on his troops, and assaulted Yangcheng with all his strength. The rebels' state was now desperate; the rebel general Yan Zheng stabbed Zhang Bao to death, presented his head, and surrendered. Zhu Jun thereupon pacified several commanderies, and submitted a memorial of victory.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The scouts return'd, and full report they made:
"[Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song) hath the rebel foe dismay'd;
[Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), oft beaten, court hath turn'd away,
And [Song](char-huangfu-song) was call'd to bear the chief's array.
When [Song](char-huangfu-song) arriv'd, [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) no more drew breath;
But [Liang](char-zhang-liang) led on his troops to face their death.
Yet seven times [Song](char-huangfu-song)'s arms triumphant led;
And [Liang](char-zhang-liang) at Quyang lost his very head.
[Jiao](char-zhang-jiao)'s coffin op'd, his corpse despoiled they tore;
The head, off-stricken, to the court they bore.
The remnant rebels yielded, every band,
And bow'd themselves to peace at his command.
The court [Song](char-huangfu-song) rais'd: Cav'lry-General named,
Of [Jizhou](loc-ji-province) Governor, by edict claimed.
Then [Song](char-huangfu-song)'s memorial spake of [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi)'s worth;
The court restored him to his former berth.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) for merit, court reward bestow'd:
Made Chancellor of Jinan — straightway he rode."
This news to [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) came; with eager band,
He pressed Yangcheng with all his armed hand.
The rebel state was now in dire distress;
Yan Zheng, a general of the rebel press,
Stabb'd [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao) through, and bore his head away,
Surrender'd, asking grace from [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun)'s sway.
[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) thus pacified the rebel band,
And sent the throne his news from war-torn land.

paragraphs.original: 時又黃巾餘黨三人，─趙弘、韓忠、孫仲─，聚眾數萬，望風燒劫，稱與張角報讎。朝廷命朱雋即以得勝之師討之。雋奉詔，率軍前進。時賊據宛城，雋引兵攻之，趙弘遣韓忠出戰。雋遣玄德、關、張攻城西南角。韓忠盡率精銳之眾，來西南角抵敵。朱雋自縱鐵騎二千，逕取東北角。賊恐失城，急棄西南而回。玄德從背後掩殺，賊眾大敗，奔入宛城。朱雋分兵四面圍定，城中斷糧，韓忠使人出城投降。雋不許。玄德曰：「昔高祖之得天下，蓋為能招降納順；公何拒韓忠耶？」雋曰：「彼一時，此一時也。昔秦項之際，天下大亂，民無定主，故招降賞附，以勸來耳。今海內一統，惟黃巾造反；若容其降，無以勸善。使賊得利恣意劫掠，失利便投降：此長寇之志，非良策也。」玄德曰：「不容寇降是矣。今四面圍如鐵桶，賊乞降不得，必然死戰，萬人一心，尚不可當，況城中有數萬死命之人乎？不若撤去東南，獨攻西北。賊必棄城而走，無心戀戰，可即擒也。」
paragraphs.prose: At that time three remnants of the Yellow Turbans—Zhao Hong, Han Zhong, and Sun Zhong—gathered some tens of thousands, plundering as the wind moved them, and proclaiming themselves avengers of Zhang Jiao. The court commanded Zhu Jun to suppress them with his victorious forces. Jun received the decree and led his troops forward. The rebels held Wancheng; Jun led his troops to attack, and Zhao Hong sent Han Zhong out to give battle. Jun ordered Xuande, Guan, and Zhang to assail the southwest corner of the city; Han Zhong led all his picked troops to defend the southwest. Zhu Jun himself charged with two thousand iron-clad cavalry directly at the northeast corner. The rebels, fearing the loss of the city, hastily abandoned the southwest and turned back. Xuande pursued from behind; the rebels were utterly defeated and fled back into Wancheng. Zhu Jun divided his forces to surround all four sides, and the city was cut off from grain. Han Zhong sent a man out to offer surrender, but Jun refused. Xuande said: "In old times when Gaozu gained the empire, it was because he could welcome submission; why does Your Excellency refuse Han Zhong?" Jun said: "That was then, this is now. In the days of Qin and Chu, the empire was in chaos and the people had no settled lord; therefore submissions were welcomed and rewarded, to encourage men to come over. Now all within the seas is one, and only the Yellow Turbans rebel; if their surrender is accepted, there is no way to encourage virtue. Were rebels, when they prosper, to plunder at will, and when they fail, to surrender—this would only feed the rebel's ambition, and is no good policy." Xuande said: "You do well not to admit the rebels' surrender. But now they are encircled as in an iron bucket; denied surrender, they will fight to the death. Ten thousand men of one heart cannot be overcome—much less when there are myriads within, sworn to die. Better to withdraw from the southeast and attack only from the northwest. The rebels will then certainly abandon the city and flee, having no heart for battle, and you may take them with ease."
paragraphs.rhyme:
Three Turban remnants still prolonged the fight:
[Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong), [Han Zhong](char-han-zhong), [Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong), strong in might,
Plunder'd the country, claiming [Jiao](char-zhang-jiao)'s lost cause;
The court bade [Jun](char-zhu-jun) set forth with little pause.
He march'd to Wancheng, where the rebel foe
Had gather'd strong; [Hong](char-zhao-hong) sent [Han Zhong](char-han-zhong) below.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) bade [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) to take the southwest gate;
Himself two-thousand-strong, the northeast straight.
[Han Zhong](char-han-zhong) his elite to the southwest drew,
To stay [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) — but [Jun](char-zhu-jun)'s charge brake right through.
The rebels, fearing all the city's loss,
Forsook the southwest, scrambling back across;
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) from rear struck hard, his men in train;
The broken foe to Wancheng fled again.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) encircled all; the city ceas'd from grain.
[Han Zhong](char-han-zhong) sent forth surrender — [Jun](char-zhu-jun) refrain'd.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) said: "[Gaozu](char-emperor-gaozu) welcom'd those who came;
Why now refuse [Han Zhong](char-han-zhong)'s submitting claim?"
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) answer'd: "Times differ; mark the change:
In Qin and [Xiang](char-xiang-yu)'s day, war filled every stage;
The realm was lordless, folk knew no firm hand,
We welcom'd those who came, that all might stand
Beneath one peaceful banner. Now the seas
Are one, and Turbans only break the ease.
Should we accept their yielded plea this day,
We could not draw men's hearts to virtue's way.
Win and they plunder; fail, they yet submit —
This breeds the rebel's hand, no statesman's wit."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied: "Thy judgment I commend;
But, fenc'd around, they'll fight until the end.
Ten thousand bound to die hold firm defense.
Withdraw the southeast — press the northwest hence;
The rebels, free to fly, will quit the field,
And, easy ta'en, to thee shall surely yield."

paragraphs.original: 雋然之，隨撤東南二面軍馬，一齊攻打西北。韓忠果引軍棄城而奔。雋與玄德、關、張率三軍掩殺，射死韓忠，餘皆四散奔走。
paragraphs.prose: Jun agreed, and at once withdrew the troops from the southeast and southern sides, and together they pressed the attack upon the northwest. Han Zhong, as expected, led his men out of the city in flight. Jun, with Xuande, Guan, and Zhang, led the three armies in close pursuit, shot Han Zhong dead, and the rest were scattered, fleeing in all directions.

paragraphs.original: 正追趕間，趙弘、孫仲引賊眾到，與雋交戰。雋見弘勢大，引軍暫退。弘乘勢復奪宛城。雋離十里下寨，方欲攻打，忽見正東一彪人馬到來。為首一將，生得廣額闊面，虎體熊腰；吳郡富春人也：姓孫，名堅，字文臺，乃孫武子之後。年十七歲，與父至錢塘，見海賊十餘人，劫取商人財物，於岸上分贓。堅謂父曰：「此賊可擒也。」遂奮力提刀上岸，揚聲大叫，東西指揮，如喚人狀。賊以為官兵至，盡棄財物奔走。堅趕上，殺一賊。由是郡縣知名，薦為校尉。後會稽妖賊許昌造反，自稱陽明皇帝，聚眾數萬；堅與郡司馬招募勇士千餘人，會合州郡破之，斬許昌并其子許韶。刺史臧旻上表奏其功，除堅為鹽瀆丞，又除盱眙丞、下邳丞。今見黃巾寇起，聚集鄉中少年及諸商旅，并淮泗精兵一千五百餘人，前來接應。
paragraphs.prose: Just as the pursuit was in progress, Zhao Hong and Sun Zhong led the rebel host up, and engaged Jun in battle. Jun, seeing Hong's force was great, withdrew his troops for a while. Hong took advantage and recaptured Wancheng. Jun encamped at a distance of ten li, and was just about to attack when suddenly from due east a column of horsemen came to view. At their head was a captain broad of brow and broad of face, tiger-bodied and bear-waisted; he was a man of Fuchun in Wu Commandery: surnamed Sun, named Jian, courtesy name Wentai—a descendant of Master Sun Wu. At seventeen years of age, when going with his father to Qiantang, he had seen more than ten sea-pirates robbing merchants and dividing the spoils on the shore. Jian said to his father: "These bandits can be seized." Whereupon, sword in hand, he sprang ashore and shouted loudly, gesturing this way and that as if calling men to him. The pirates, supposing that government troops had come, abandoned their plunder and fled. Jian gave chase and slew one of them. Thereby his name became known in the commandery and county, and he was recommended as Colonel. Later, when the demon-rebel Xu Chang of Kuaiji rose in revolt, calling himself the Yangming Emperor and gathering tens of thousands, Jian, together with the Marshal of the commandery, mustered over a thousand brave men, joined the forces of province and commandery, and broke the rebels, beheading Xu Chang and his son Xu Shao. The Inspector Zang Min memorialized his merit, and Jian was appointed Assistant of Yandu, and afterwards Assistant of Xuyi and of Xiapi. Now, seeing the Yellow Turban rebellion break out, he had gathered the youth of his village and the various merchants, together with more than fifteen hundred elite troops from the Huai-Si region, and was come to lend his support.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Mid pursuit, [Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong), [Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) came in train,
And met [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) upon the battle's plain.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) saw the foe outnumber'd him, withdrew;
And [Hong](char-zhao-hong), in vict'ry, Wancheng took anew.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) pitch'd ten li away, to gather might;
About to strike — when, from the eastward sight,
A horse-band came; the leader, fierce and bold,
Broad-brow'd, wide-fac'd, bear-loin'd, with tiger's mold.
From Fuchun, Wu, [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) of Han was born;
Of Sun Wu's stem — [Wentai](char-sun-jian) the style he'd worn.
At seventeen, with father he had gone
To Qiantang's shore; where, looking thereupon,
A dozen pirates more were sharing spoil
From plunder'd merchants in their lawless toil.
Said [Jian](char-sun-jian) to father: "These may be ta'en in hand!"
And with his blade he jumped upon the strand.
He shouted high, gestur'd to east and west,
As though to call great hosts unto his quest;
The pirates, fearing officers had come,
Forsook the spoils and fled in panic dumb.
[Jian](char-sun-jian) gave them chase, one rogue before him fell;
His name through commanderies wide spread well.
Acclaim'd a Colonel by the country's voice,
He rose to rank, the realm's distinguish'd choice.
In Kuaiji, warlock Xu Chang rebellion play'd;
Self-styl'd 'Yangming Emp'ror' — myriads array'd.
[Jian](char-sun-jian), with the Marshal of his region, rais'd
A thousand swords, with state and shire array'd.
With province' aid the rebels' line was broke;
Xu Chang and son both perish'd by the stroke.
Inspector Zang Min praised [Jian](char-sun-jian)'s daring deed,
And memorialized him for further need;
Post of Yandu Assistant first he gain'd,
And Xuyi, Xiapi too his rise sustain'd.
Now hearing of the Yellow Turbans' rage,
[Jian](char-sun-jian) gather'd village youth and merchants sage,
Plus fifteen hundred Huai-Si troops in train,
And march'd to lend his arm to the campaign.

paragraphs.original: 朱雋大喜，便令堅攻打南門，玄德打北門，朱雋打西門，留東門與賊走。孫堅首先登城，斬賊二十餘人，賊眾奔潰。趙弘飛馬突槊，直取孫堅。堅從城上飛身奪弘槊，刺弘下馬；卻騎弘馬，飛身往來殺賊。孫仲引賊突出北門，正迎玄德，無心戀戰，只待奔逃。玄德張弓一箭，正中孫仲，翻身落馬。朱雋大軍，隨後掩殺，斬首數萬級，降者不可勝計。南陽一路，十數郡皆平。雋班師回京,詔封為車騎對軍，河南尹。雋表奏孫堅、劉備等功。堅有人情，除別郡司馬上任去了；惟玄德聽候日久，不得除授。
paragraphs.prose: Zhu Jun was greatly pleased, and at once ordered Jian to attack the south gate, Xuande the north, and himself the west, leaving the east gate open for the rebels to flee. Sun Jian was the first to mount the wall, slaying more than twenty of the rebels, and the rebel host fell into rout. Zhao Hong, on a swift horse with leveled lance, came charging straight at Sun Jian. Jian leapt down from the wall, seized Hong's lance, ran him through, and toppled him from his saddle; then, mounting Hong's own horse, he flew here and there cutting down the rebels. Sun Zhong led his men to break out at the north gate, where he came face to face with Xuande; having no heart for battle, he was bent only upon flight. Xuande drew his bow and shot one arrow, which struck Sun Zhong full, and he toppled from his horse. Zhu Jun's main army pursued from behind, beheading tens of thousands, and those who surrendered were beyond reckoning. Along the road of Nanyang, more than ten commanderies were pacified. Jun returned with his army to the capital, where by edict he was made General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Prefect of Henan. He memorialized to court the merits of Sun Jian, Liu Bei, and the others. Jian, having connections at court, was appointed Marshal of another commandery and departed to take up his post; but Xuande, waiting long for an appointment, was not advanced.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), well-pleas'd, the gates assign'd around:
[Jian](char-sun-jian) to the south, [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) the north was bound,
Himself to west; the east he left as way
For rebels' flight, that they might haste away.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) first scaled the rampart at the call;
He slew full twenty; rebels fled the wall.
[Zhao Hong](char-zhao-hong), with lance, on horseback charg'd [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian);
[Jian](char-sun-jian) leapt from wall, and snatch'd the lance amain.
He pierc'd [Hong](char-zhao-hong) through, who toppled to the ground;
On [Hong](char-zhao-hong)'s own horse, slew rebels all around.
[Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) his rebels at the north out broke;
There met [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), who barr'd them with a stroke.
The rebel chief, no heart for battle, sought
Through flight to save his life, by panic caught.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) drew bow, with arrow swift and true;
[Sun Zhong](char-sun-zhong) was struck, and from his horse he flew.
[Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) pursu'd; the rebel ranks were slain;
Some myriads dead, surrenders past explain.
In Nanyang, commanderies ten he freed;
The rebel host destroy'd in mighty deed.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun), led to capital, the throne addressed,
Where with high titles was his merit blessed:
As Cav'lry-General, by court's command,
And Prefect of Henan, with honor'd hand.
[Jun](char-zhu-jun) praised the merits of his loyal men:
[Jian](char-sun-jian), with court connections, was advanc'd, and then
Made Marshal of another commandery's stand;
But [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) waited long, no rank in hand.

paragraphs.original: 三人鬱鬱不樂，上街閒行，正值郎中張鈞車到。玄德見之，自陳功績。鈞大驚，隨入朝見帝曰：「昔黃巾造反，其原皆由十常侍賣官鬻爵，非親不用，非讎不誅，以致天下大亂。今宜斬十常侍，懸首南郊，遣使者布告天下，有功者重加賞賜，則四海自清平也。」十常侍奏帝曰：「張鈞欺主。」帝令武士逐出張鈞。十常侍共議：「此必破黃巾有功者，不得除授，故生怨言。權且教省家銓注微名，待後卻再理會未晚。」因此玄德除授定州中山府安喜縣尉，剋日赴任。玄德將兵散回鄉里，止帶親隨二十餘人，與關、張來安喜縣中到任。署縣事一月，與民秋毫無犯，民皆感化。到任之後，與關、張食則同桌，寢則同床。如玄德在稠人廣坐，關、張侍立，終日不倦。
paragraphs.prose: The three were sad and unhappy, and as they walked idly through the streets, the carriage of the Court Counselor Zhang Jun chanced to come by. Xuande saw him, and himself related his services. Zhang Jun was greatly amazed, and forthwith entered the court and addressed the Emperor: "When the Yellow Turbans rose in rebellion, the root of it lay all in this—that the Ten Attendants sold offices and titles; none save their kin were employed, none save their foes were punished, until the empire fell into chaos. The Ten Attendants should now be beheaded, their heads hung in the southern suburbs, and envoys dispatched to proclaim it throughout the realm; those of merit should be richly rewarded, and then the four seas will of themselves be at peace." The Ten Attendants thereupon reported to the Emperor: "Zhang Jun deceives Your Majesty." The Emperor commanded his guards to drive Zhang Jun forth. The Ten Attendants conferred together: "This must be one of those who, having earned merit in breaking the Yellow Turbans, has been denied his post and now complains. Let us have the secretariat enroll him in some minor place; we may attend to him hereafter." On this account Xuande was appointed Defender of Anxi County, in Zhongshan Prefecture of Dingzhou, and ordered to take up his post forthwith. Xuande dismissed his troops to return to their villages, and, with only some twenty personal followers, set out with Guan and Zhang for Anxi County. Within a month of taking office, he had not done the people the smallest injury, and all the populace were moved by his rule. Thereafter, he ate with Guan and Zhang at the same table, and slept on the same couch; and when Xuande sat among assemblies, Guan and Zhang stood attending all day without weariness.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The three, in sadness, idly walk'd the street;
There Zhang Jun's car came rolling by — they meet.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) address'd him, told his service plain;
The deeds of war, but yet, no rank to gain.
Jun, much amaz'd, to court at once repair'd,
And to the throne his counsel forth declar'd:
"The Yellow Turbans rose against the throne;
Their cause: the Ten Attendants, who alone
Sold office to their kin, struck down their foe;
And brought the realm to chaos and to woe.
Behead the Ten — expose their heads, and lead
The realm by edict to redress the deed;
Reward the worthy, that the realm grow strong;
And four seas' peace shall rise, and last full long."
The Ten alarm'd, address'd the throne in dread:
"Zhang Jun deceives Your Majesty," they said.
The King, persuaded, bade his guards expel
Zhang Jun forthwith; and so his counsel fell.
The Ten conferr'd: "This wretch some hero be,
Who broke the Turbans, balk'd of proper fee.
Place but his name in office, low and small;
We'll deal with him hereafter, when chance befall."
They gave [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) Anxi's Defender's seat,
And bade him march his minor charge to meet.
He sent his troops to homes; some score retain'd,
And with [Guan](char-guan-yu), [Zhang](char-zhang-fei) to Anxi's seat attain'd.
In office one month past, no slight he wrought
The people; all were mov'd by virtue's thought.
With [Guan](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang](char-zhang-fei) one table still he kept,
And on one couch the three together slept.
When [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) sat in hall with crowded throng,
[Guan](char-guan-yu), [Zhang](char-zhang-fei) stood by attendant all day long.

paragraphs.original: 到縣未及四月，朝廷降詔，凡有軍功為長吏者當沙汰。玄德疑在遣中。適督郵行部至縣，玄德出郭迎接，見督郵施禮。督郵坐於馬上，惟微以鞭指回答。關、張二公俱怒。及到館驛，督郵南面高坐，玄德侍立階下。良久，督郵問曰：「劉縣尉是何出身？」玄德曰：「備乃中山靖王之後；自涿郡剿戮黃巾，大小三十餘戰，頗有微功，因得除今職。」督郵大喝曰：「汝詐稱皇親，虛報功績！目今朝廷降詔，正要沙汰這等濫官汙吏！」玄德喏喏連聲而退。歸到縣中，與縣吏商議。吏曰：「督郵入威，無非要賄賂耳。」玄德曰：「我與民秋毫無犯，那得財物與他？」次日，督郵先提縣吏去，勒令指稱縣尉害民。玄德幾番自往求免，俱被門役阻住，不肯放參。
paragraphs.prose: He had been at the county not yet four months when the court issued an edict, by which all who held senior office through military merit were to be culled out. Xuande suspected he might be among those to be sent away. It chanced that the Postal Inspector came to the county upon his tour. Xuande went out of the city to receive him and saluted him with due ceremony; but the Postal Inspector sat on horseback and merely pointed lightly with his whip in reply. Guan and Zhang were both kindled with anger. When they reached the courier-lodge, the Postal Inspector sat in the place of honor, facing south, while Xuande stood attending below the steps. After a long while, the Postal Inspector inquired: "What is the lineage of Defender Liu?" Xuande said: "I, Bei, am descended from Prince Jing of Zhongshan; from Zhuo Commandery I joined to suppress the Yellow Turbans through more than thirty battles, great and small, and won some little merit, by which I was given my present office." The Postal Inspector roared aloud: "You falsely claim imperial kinship and report fictitious services! At this very time the court has issued an edict precisely to cull such grasping and corrupt officials!" Xuande, with submissive 'Yes! yes!' withdrew. Returning to the county office, he took counsel with the clerk. The clerk said: "The Inspector's high airs are no more than a demand for bribes." Xuande said: "I have not done the people the smallest harm; what means have I to give him?" On the next day, the Inspector first had the clerk seized, and pressed him to swear that the County Defender had injured the people. Xuande went several times in person to ask for his release, but was held back at the gate by the runners, who would not let him pass.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Scarce four months pass'd at Anxi, when there came
An edict from the throne, of dreaded name:
That those by martial merit rais'd in rank
Should now be cull'd, their offices made blank.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) suspected he among them sank.
It chanc'd the Postal Inspector came in tour;
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) went forth, beyond the city's door.
He kept his saddle, with his whip on high,
And lightly pointed [Bei](char-liu-bei) a slight reply.
[Guan](char-guan-yu), [Zhang](char-zhang-fei), beholding both, were fill'd with ire,
And both their hearts within them burn'd like fire.
The Inspector took the lodge's southern seat;
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) stood at the steps below his feet.
At length the Inspector ask'd him, with scorn:
"Defender [Liu](char-liu-bei), of what descent art born?"
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied: "Of Zhongshan's princely line
I sprung, the Han imperial blood is mine;
In [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) I join'd the war 'gainst rebel roar,
And bore some merit through the bloody store.
Some thirty battles fought, both small and great;
By which I won this present low estate."
The Inspector roar'd: "Thou falsely state
Imperial blood — and false thy deeds relate!
The court hath issu'd edict at this hour,
To purge such grasping wretches of their pow'r!"
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) with humble bow, gave brief assent,
And from the chamber meekly so he went.
Return'd, with clerk he weigh'd the matter o'er.
"These airs," said clerk, "are bribes — and nothing more."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied: "I have not wrong'd the folk;
What goods have I to satisfy his yoke?"
Next day, the chief seiz'd up the clerk in chains,
And forc'd him to declare [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s foul stains.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) went oft to ask the clerk's release;
But door-attendants barr'd, and bade him cease.

paragraphs.original: 郤說張飛飲了數盃悶酒，乘馬從館驛前過，見五六十個老人，皆在門前痛哭。飛問其故。眾老人答曰：「督郵逼勒縣吏，欲害劉公；我等皆來苦告，不得放入，反遭把門人趕打！」張飛大怒，睜圓環眼，咬碎鋼牙，滾鞍下馬，逕入館驛，把門人那裏阻擋得住。直奔後堂，見督郵正坐廳上，將縣吏綁倒在地。飛大喝：「害民賊！認得我麼？」督郵未及開言，早被張飛揪住頭髮，扯出館驛，直到縣前馬樁上縛住；扳下柳條，去督郵兩腿上著力鞭打，一連打折柳條十數枝。
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of Zhang Fei, who, having drunk several cups of melancholy wine, was riding past the front of the post-station when he saw fifty or sixty old men weeping bitterly before its gate. Fei asked them the reason. The old men answered, "The Postal Inspector is pressing the county clerk, seeking to do harm to Lord Liu; we have all come to plead bitterly, but were not allowed to enter, and were instead beaten away by the gatekeepers!" Zhang Fei was greatly enraged, his round eyes opened wide, his steel teeth gnashed to splinters; he rolled from the saddle and dismounted, and went straight into the post-station — the gatekeepers could not bar him. He charged into the rear hall and saw the Postal Inspector seated upon the dais, with the county clerk bound and thrown upon the ground. Fei thundered, "Bandit, who harms the people! Do you know me?" Before the Postal Inspector could open his mouth, Zhang Fei had already seized him by the hair, dragged him out of the post-station, and bound him fast to the hitching-post in front of the county yamen; he tore down willow branches, and beat the Postal Inspector with all his strength upon both legs, breaking more than ten willow rods one after another.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Now [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), drowning sorrows in his wine,
Rode past the post, and saw a mournful line:
Some fifty greybeards weeping at the gate.
He ask'd; they answer'd: "Cruel is our state!
The wretch is pressing hard the county clerk,
To do Lord [Liu](char-liu-bei) some harm by hidden work.
We came to plead — they barr'd us from the door,
And drove us off with blows, and bruis'd us sore!"
At this [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), in fury, flash'd his eyes,
His teeth he gnash'd, his rage out-leap'd the skies;
He sprang from saddle, storming in amain;
No gateman might his rushing stride detain.
Straight to the hall, the Inspector he found,
With clerk in cords beneath, upon the ground.
"Thou bane of folk!" [Fei](char-zhang-fei) cried, "know'st thou my name?"
By hair he seiz'd him, ere a word could frame.
And dragg'd him forth beyond the hostel-pale,
To bind him fast upon the hitching-rail.
Tore willow branches, lash'd with all his might,
His legs he beat, the lashes firm and tight;
And one by one, the willow rods were broke,
A dozen splinter'd 'neath each thund'rous stroke.

paragraphs.original: 玄德正納悶間，聽得縣前喧鬧，問左右，答曰：「張將軍綁一人在縣前痛打。」玄德忙去觀之，見綁縛者乃督郵也。玄德驚問其故。飛曰：「此等害民賊，不打死等甚！」督郵告曰：「玄德公救我性命！」玄德終是仁慈的人，急喝張飛住手。傍邊轉過關公來，曰：「兄長建許多大功，僅得縣尉，今反被督郵侮辱。吾思枳棘叢中，非棲鸞鳳之所；不如殺督郵，棄官歸鄉，別圖遠大之計。」玄德乃取印綬，掛於督郵之頸，責之曰：「據汝害民，本當殺卻；今姑饒汝命。吾繳還印綬，從此去矣！」督郵歸告定州太守，太守申文省府，差人捕捉。玄德、關、張三人往代州投劉恢。恢見玄德乃漢室宗親，留匿在家不題。
paragraphs.prose: Xuande was just sitting in melancholy when he heard a clamor before the county yamen. He asked his attendants, who answered, "General Zhang has bound a man before the county and is beating him fiercely." Xuande hurried to look, and saw that the man bound was the Postal Inspector. Xuande, alarmed, asked the reason. Fei said, "Such a bandit who harms the people — what good is it not to beat him to death?" The Postal Inspector pleaded, "Lord Xuande, save my life!" Xuande was, after all, a man of benevolence, and at once shouted to Zhang Fei to hold his hand. Lord Guan stepped forward from the side and said, "Elder brother, having achieved so many great merits, you have gained only a County Defender's post, and now are besides this insulted by a Postal Inspector. I think that thickets of thorn and bramble are no place for the phoenix to roost; better to kill the Postal Inspector, abandon the office, return to our native place, and lay other and greater plans." Xuande then took up his seal and ribbon, hung it about the Postal Inspector's neck, and rebuked him, saying, "By rights, for your harm to the people, you ought to be put to death; but now I spare your life. I return the seal and ribbon, and from this hour depart!" The Postal Inspector returned and reported to the Grand Administrator of Dingzhou, and the Grand Administrator submitted a memorial to the provincial offices, dispatching men to apprehend them. Xuande, Lord Guan, and Zhang Fei, the three of them, made for Daizhou and sought shelter with Liu Hui. Hui, seeing that Xuande was a kinsman of the Han imperial house, kept him hidden in his home — but of this, no more.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) sat troubled when, before the gate,
A din arose; he ask'd the cause and state.
"Lord [Zhang](char-zhang-fei)," they said, "hath seiz'd a wretch in chains,
And 'fore the court is dealing fiery pains."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) flew forth, beheld the captive's face —
The Postal Inspector, bound in dire disgrace!
He gasp'd, and ask'd the reason; [Fei](char-zhang-fei) replied,
"This bane of folk — let blows be not deny'd!"
"Lord [Xuande](char-liu-bei)!" the captive cried, "save my life!"
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), whose heart abhorr'd all needless strife,
Bade [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) stay his hand. [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) drew near,
And spake aside: "My brother, mark and hear:
Thy many deeds have brought thee but a post,
Where now this knave hath flouted thee the most.
The thorny brake's no roost for phoenix wing —
Far better slay this dog, resign the ring,
Then home return, and shape some broader aim."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) drew forth the seal — laid down his claim.
And round the captive's neck the seal he tied,
Then to the wretch, in stern rebuke, he cried:
"For harms to folk, thy life were due to fall;
Yet now I spare it — let this end thy gall.
The seal I yield, the office I forsake,
And from this hour my own free way I take."
The wretch to Dingzhou's chief made known his case;
Who to the province writ, and sent the chase.
But to Daizhou the brothers' flight was bent,
Where Liu Hui took them in, his lodging lent.
He saw [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) was Han's own kindred true,
And hid him fast — no more we shall pursue.

paragraphs.original: 卻說十常侍既握重權，互相商議：但有不從己者，誅之。趙忠，張讓，差人問破黃巾將士索金帛，不從者奏罷職。皇甫嵩、朱雋皆不肯與，趙忠等俱奏罷其官。帝又封趙忠等為車騎將軍，張讓等十三人皆封列侯。朝政愈壞，人民嗟怨。於是長沙賊區星作亂；漁陽張舉、張純反：舉稱天子，純稱大將軍。表章雪片告急，十常侍皆藏匿不奏。
paragraphs.prose: Now to tell of the Ten Permanent Attendants, who, having now grasped great power, took counsel among themselves: any who would not bend to them, they would put to death. Zhao Zhong and Zhang Rang sent men to demand gold and silk from the generals and officers who had broken the Yellow Turbans; those who refused they memorialized to be dismissed from office. Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun both refused to give, and Zhao Zhong and his fellows together memorialized to have them stripped of their posts. The Emperor further enfeoffed Zhao Zhong and the others as Generals of Chariots and Cavalry, and ennobled Zhang Rang and twelve more — thirteen men in all — as ranked marquises. The government of the court grew daily worse, and the common people groaned in grievance. Whereupon Qu Xing, a bandit of Changsha, rose in rebellion; and Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun of Yuyang revolted — Ju styling himself Son of Heaven, and Chun calling himself Grand General. Memorials of urgent peril fell thick as snow, but the Ten Permanent Attendants concealed them all and would not present them to the throne.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The Ten Attendants, vested deep in might,
Took counsel: who oppos'd them, slay outright.
[Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong), [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), sent men for plunder's sake,
To wring from victors gold and silk to take.
And those who balk'd, by writ they cast aside,
From rank and honour straightway were deny'd.
[Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), who scorn'd to yield up gold,
By writ from [Zhao](char-zhao-zhong) were stripp'd of office's hold.
Th' Emperor made [Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong) cav'lry-chief,
And rais'd [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) with twelve to titled fief.
The court grew daily worse; the people groan'd,
And bitter sorrow through the realm was moan'd.
Then Qu Xing, robber-chief of Changsha land,
And Yuyang's twain, Zhang Ju, Zhang Chun, took stand;
Ju styl'd himself the Son of Heaven proud,
Chun rais'd Grand General's standard, fierce and loud.
The urgent scrolls fell thick, like flakes of snow;
But hid by Ten that throne might never know.

paragraphs.original: 一日，帝在後園與十常侍飲宴，諫議大夫劉陶，逕到帝前大慟。帝問其故。陶曰：「天下危在旦夕，陛下尚自與閹官共飲耶！」帝曰：「國家承平，有何危急？」陶曰：「四方盜賊並起，侵掠州郡。其禍皆由十常侍賣官害民，欺君罔上。朝廷正人皆去，禍在目前矣！」十常侍皆免冠跪伏於帝前曰：「大臣不相容，臣等不能活矣！願乞性命歸田里，盡將家產以助軍資。」言罷痛哭。帝怒謂陶曰：「汝亦有近侍之人，何獨不容朕耶？」呼武士推出斬之。劉陶大呼：「臣死不惜！可憐漢室天下，四百餘年，到此一旦休矣！」
paragraphs.prose: One day, the Emperor was drinking and feasting with the Ten Permanent Attendants in the rear garden, when the Grand Counselor Liu Tao came straight up before him and broke into loud weeping. The Emperor asked the reason. Tao said, "The empire stands in peril from morning to evening, and Your Majesty still drinks with eunuchs!" The Emperor said, "The state is at peace — what danger is there?" Tao said, "Bandits and robbers are rising on every side, plundering the provinces and commanderies. The calamity comes wholly from the Ten Permanent Attendants selling office, harming the people, deceiving Your Majesty and concealing matters from above. The upright men in the court have all departed, and disaster is now before our eyes!" The Ten Permanent Attendants all removed their caps and knelt prostrate before the Emperor, saying, "If the great minister will not tolerate us, we cannot live! We beg leave to give up our lives and return to our fields, and to give all our household property to help with military supplies." Having spoken, they wept bitterly. The Emperor, angered, said to Tao, "You too have your own attendants beside you — why is it that you alone will not tolerate Us?" He called the guards to drag him out and behead him. Liu Tao cried out, "I do not grudge to die! Pity only the Han house's realm — over four hundred years, ended on this single day!"
paragraphs.rhyme:
One day, the king, beside the Ten, sat down,
In rear-park feast — they laugh'd, the wine flow'd round.
When forth came Tao, the Counselor of state,
And wept before the king in piteous rate.
The throne enquir'd; Liu Tao began to plead:
"The realm now totters, perilous indeed —
Yet still doth Sire with eunuchs sit and dine!"
The throne return'd: "Where is this peril's sign?"
"On every side the bandit-bands arise,
Plund'ring the lands and towns with savage cries.
The fault is theirs — those Ten, who sell command,
Who rob the folk, and cheat the throne unmann'd;
The upright men of court have fled away;
Calamity is here this very day!"
The Ten Attendants doff'd their caps, on knee,
And wail'd: "If thus this lord our doom decree,
We cannot live! Yet take our home, our store,
Our jewels, all to swell the army's war;
Then to the fields, as common men, we'll fly,
We crave but life — no other suit apply."
So spake they all, with bitter weeping show,
And tears upon their cheeks were freely strown.
In wrath the throne reply'd: "Thou hast thine own —
Why hate Our train, of all men, thou alone?"
He bade his guards lay hands on Tao straightway,
And drag him forth, to slay without delay.
Liu Tao cried loud: "No grief I bear to die!
But weep for Han, that holds the realm so high,
Four hundred years — and now in one day's pall,
Has seen its noble house in ruin fall!"

paragraphs.original: 武士擁陶出，方欲行刑，一大臣喝住曰：「勿得下手，待我諫去。」眾視之，乃司徒陳耽。逕入室中來諫帝曰：「劉諫議得何罪而受誅？」帝曰：「毀謗近臣，冒朕躬。」耽曰：「天下人民，欲食十常侍之肉，陛下敬之如父母，身無寸功，皆封列侯；況封諝等結連黃巾，欲為內亂：陛下今不自省，社稷立見崩摧矣！」帝曰：「封諝作亂，其事不明。十常侍中，豈無一二忠臣？」陳耽以頭撞階而諫。帝怒，命牽出，與劉陶皆下獄。是夜，十常侍即於獄中謀殺之；假帝韶以孫堅為長沙太守，討區星。
paragraphs.prose: The guards hustled Tao out and were just about to carry out the execution, when a great minister called out and stayed them, "Stay your hands; let me go and remonstrate." All looked, and it was Minister of the Masses Chen Dan. He went straight into the inner chamber to remonstrate with the Emperor, saying, "By what crime has Counselor Liu been condemned to death?" The Emperor said, "He slandered Our near attendants and offended Our own person." Dan said, "All the people of the empire wish to eat the flesh of the Ten Permanent Attendants, yet Your Majesty honors them as a father and mother. Though they have not an inch of merit, they are all enfeoffed as ranked marquises; and what is more, Feng Xu and his fellows have joined hands with the Yellow Turbans and are plotting inner rebellion. If Your Majesty does not look into this, the altars of the realm will be seen to crumble before our eyes!" The Emperor said, "Feng Xu's rebellion is not clear; among the Ten Permanent Attendants, surely there must be one or two loyal men?" Chen Dan struck his head against the stone steps in remonstrance. The Emperor, enraged, ordered him dragged out, and together with Liu Tao both were sent to prison. That night, the Ten Permanent Attendants plotted to murder them in their cells; and they counterfeited an imperial edict appointing Sun Jian as Grand Administrator of Changsha, to chastise Qu Xing.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The guards bore Tao away to take his head,
When forth a minister, with shout, thus said:
"Hold off your hands! Let me first remonstrate!"
All look'd: 'twas Chen Dan, Minister of state.
Within he came, and to the king he spake:
"What crime hath made Liu Tao his life forsake?"
The throne reply'd: "He slander'd Our own train,
And brav'd Our person with a tongue profane."
Dan said: "The people throughout Han's broad land
Would eat the flesh of those Ten Servants' band;
Yet you esteem them like a parent dear,
Though not one inch of merit doth appear;
Yet are they all enfeoff'd as marquis-lords,
And rais'd above the realm by guilty cords.
Nay more — [Feng Xu](char-feng-xu) with others, plotting bold,
Have join'd the Yellow Turbans, ills untold;
If Sire amend not, soon the kingdom dies,
And altars topple 'fore Your Highness' eyes!"
The throne return'd: "[Feng Xu](char-feng-xu)'s revolt's not plain;
Are none among the Ten of loyal strain?"
Chen Dan with grief against the marble flew,
And smote his head — but pleas no answer drew.
The throne, in wrath, commanded: "Take him hence,
To prison send him, with Liu Tao's offence!"
That very night, the Ten Attendants sped
To plot their murder in the prison-bed;
And forg'd an edict in their lord's high name:
To [Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) Changsha's chiefdom they proclaim;
His charge, against Qu Xing, with force to wage,
To slay the rebel, calm the troubled stage.

paragraphs.original: 不五十日，報捷，江夏平。詔封堅為烏程侯；封劉虞為幽州牧，領兵往漁陽征張舉、張純。代州劉恢以書薦玄德見虞。虞大喜，令玄德為都尉，引兵直抵賊巢，與賊大戰數日，挫動銳氣。張純專一兇暴，士卒心變，帳下頭目刺殺張純，將頭納獻，率眾來降。張舉見勢敗，亦自縊死。漁陽盡平。劉虞表奏劉備大功，朝廷赦免鞭督郵之罪，除下密丞，遷高堂尉。公孫瓚又表陳玄德前功，薦為別部司馬，守平原縣令。玄德在平原，頗有錢糧軍馬，重整舊日氣象。劉虞平寇有功，封太尉。
paragraphs.prose: In not fifty days, victory was reported: Jiangxia had been pacified. The court enfeoffed Sun Jian as Marquis of Wucheng, and made Liu Yu Governor of Youzhou, ordering him to lead troops to Yuyang to attack Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun. Liu Hui of Daizhou wrote a letter recommending Xuande to Liu Yu. Liu Yu was greatly pleased, and made Xuande a Commandant, leading troops directly to the rebels' lair. He fought great battles for several days, blunting the rebels' fierce spirit. Zhang Chun, ferocious and tyrannical, had estranged his soldiers' hearts; one of his own staff captains stabbed him dead, presented his head, and surrendered with all the troops. Zhang Ju, seeing the cause was lost, hanged himself. Yuyang was wholly pacified. Liu Yu submitted a memorial reporting Liu Bei's great merit; the court pardoned him for the offense of whipping the Postal Inspector, appointed him Assistant of Xiami County, and afterward promoted him to Defender of Gaotang. Gongsun Zan in turn submitted a memorial setting forth Liu Bei's earlier deeds, and recommended him as Detachment Marshal, with charge as Magistrate of Pingyuan County. While in Pingyuan, Liu Bei had ample funds, grain, and horses, and once again restored the bearing of his former days. Liu Yu, for his merit in pacifying the rebels, was enfeoffed as Grand Commandant.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In fifty days came tidings of success:
Jiangxia was tam'd, the rebels in distress.
[Sun Jian](char-sun-jian) to Wucheng's Marquis-rank was rais'd;
[Liu Yu](char-liu-yu), [Youzhou](loc-you-province)'s seal, with honors prais'd,
With orders to Yuyang to lead the way,
'Gainst Zhang Ju, Zhang Chun and their rebel sway.
Liu Hui from Daizhou unto [Liu Yu](char-liu-yu) sent
A letter, [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s service to commend.
[Liu Yu](char-liu-yu) rejoic'd, and [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s worth approved;
As Commandant, with troops he onward moved.
Strait to the rebel-lair the troops he led;
For days they fought, till rebel sharpness fled.
Zhang Chun, whose savage rule his soldiers tore,
Was by a captain stabb’d, and lived no more;
His sever’d head the rebel captain gave,
And led the host to yield, their lives to save.
Zhang Ju, the cause now lost, by rope was found
To take his life: Yuyang in peace was bound.
[Liu Yu](char-liu-yu) to court reported [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s deed;
The court forgave the whipping by decree.
Assistant first at Xiami was his post;
Then Gaotang's Defender next he rose.
[Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan), too, with writ of friendly tone,
Recall'd [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei)'s old service to the throne:
Detachment Marshal was his rank assigned;
And Pingyuan's Magistrate his charge combined.
Now [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) held in Pingyuan ample store
Of gold and grain, and stood as once before.
[Liu Yu](char-liu-yu), for quelling rebels, won the chair
Of Grand Commandant by imperial care.

paragraphs.original: 中平六年，夏四月，靈帝病篤，召大將軍何進入宮，商議後事。那何進起身屠家；因妹入宮為貴人，生皇子辯，遂立為皇后，進由是得權重任。帝又寵幸王美人，生皇子協。何后嫉妒，鴆殺王美人。皇子協養於董太后宮中。董太后乃靈帝之母，解瀆亭侯劉萇之妻也。初因桓帝無子，迎立解瀆亭侯之子，是為靈帝。靈帝入繼大統，遂迎養母氏於宮中，尊為太后。
paragraphs.prose: In the sixth year of Zhongping, in the fourth month of summer, Emperor Ling lay gravely ill, and summoned the Grand General He Jin into the palace to consult upon the affairs of succession. He Jin had risen from a butcher's house; because his sister had entered the palace as an Honored Lady and borne Prince Bian, she had been made Empress, and through this He Jin had gained great power. The Emperor also doted upon Lady Wang, who bore him Prince Xie. Empress He, in jealousy, poisoned Lady Wang. Prince Xie was raised in the palace of Empress Dowager Dong. Empress Dowager Dong was Emperor Ling's mother, the wife of Liu Chang, Marquis of Jiedu Pavilion. Originally, because Emperor Huan had no son, the son of the Marquis of Jiedu Pavilion was raised up to the throne — and this was Emperor Ling. Once Emperor Ling had succeeded to the great line, he brought his mother into the palace and honored her with the title of Empress Dowager.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In [Zhongping](misc-zhongping)'s sixth year, in the fourth month's tide,
[Emperor Ling](char-emperor-ling) lay sick — his end drew nigh.
He sent for [He Jin](char-he-jin), Grand General of state,
To counsel with him on the throne's estate.
[He Jin](char-he-jin) had risen from a butcher's stall;
His sister, drawn into the palace-hall,
Was Honor'd Lady made; she bore [Prince Bian](char-prince-bian),
And so was queen'd — [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s high pow'r began.
The Emperor favour'd Lady Wang beside;
She bore [Prince Xie](char-prince-xie), the younger royal pride.
But [Empress He](char-empress-he), by jealous fury led,
With poison struck, and Lady Wang lay dead.
[Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) was rear'd in [Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong)'s own halls;
She was [Ling](char-emperor-ling)'s mother, hous'd in courtly walls,
Wife of Liu Chang, Jiedu Pavilion's chief;
Since Emperor Huan had left no son behind,
Liu Chang's own son was to the throne assigned.
He brought his mother to the palace gate,
As [Empress Dowager](char-empress-dowager-dong) — most high in state.

paragraphs.original: 董太后嘗勸帝立皇子協為太子。帝亦偏愛協，欲立之。當時病篤，中常侍蹇碩奏曰：「若欲立協，必先誅何進，以絕後患。」帝然其說，因宣進入宮。進至宮門，司馬潘隱謂進曰：「不可入宮：蹇碩欲謀殺公。」進大驚，急歸私宅，召諸大臣，欲盡誅宦官。座上一人挺身百出曰：「宦官之勢，起自沖、質之時；朝廷滋蔓極廣，安能盡誅？倘機不密，必有滅族之禍：請細詳之。」進視之，乃典軍校尉曹操也。進叱曰：「汝小輩安知朝廷大事！」
paragraphs.prose: The Empress Dowager Dong had often urged the Emperor to make Prince Xie the Crown Prince. The Emperor too was partial to Xie, and wished to install him. At that time, gravely ill, the Permanent Attendant Jian Shuo memorialized, saying, "If you would install Xie, you must first have He Jin put to death, to cut off all later peril." The Emperor agreed, and so summoned He Jin into the palace. He Jin came to the palace gate; the Marshal Pan Yin said to him, "Do not enter the palace: Jian Shuo plots to murder you, my lord." He Jin, greatly alarmed, hastened back to his private residence, and called all the great ministers, intending to put all the eunuchs to death. From among those seated, one stepped forth and said, "The eunuchs' power had its rise in the time of Emperors Chong and Zhi; their branches and roots within the court are spread exceedingly wide — how can they all be put to death? If the design is not closely kept, there must come the calamity of clan-extermination. Pray you consider it carefully." He Jin looked at him: it was Cao Cao, the Colonel of the Standing Army. He Jin scolded him, saying, "What does a junior like you know of the great affairs of court!"
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dowager Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) oft urged, with anxious care,
That [Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) be declared the lawful heir.
The [Emperor](char-emperor-ling) too, who held [Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) most dear,
Inclined to set him next in order clear.
But, while the king lay sick, [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) arose:
"If [Xie](char-prince-xie) be heir, then [He Jin](char-he-jin) too must close
His life — else after-trouble dare appear."
The king assented; summon'd [He Jin](char-he-jin) near.
[He Jin](char-he-jin) came to the gate; Pan Yin he met,
Who whisper'd low: "Go not — thy life beset!
[Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) within hath set a murd'rous snare;
Turn back, my lord, from this most fatal lair."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) sped home in haste; his men he sought,
Convening all the ministers of court;
Resolved at once to slay the eunuch train;
But one stood forth, and spoke in cautious strain:
"Their pow'r arose in Chong's and Zhi's old reign;
Through all the court its branches spread amain.
How can they all be slain by one decree?
If plot leak out, our clans in ruin sleep.
Pray ponder!" said the speaker; [He Jin](char-he-jin) then
Beheld [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) — Standard-Colonel, then.
[He Jin](char-he-jin) in scorn rebuk'd: "Thou youngster bold,
What know'st thou of the matters elders hold?"

paragraphs.original: 正躊躇間，潘隱至，言：「帝已崩。今蹇碩與十常侍商議，秘不發喪，矯詔宣何國舅入宮，欲絕後患，冊立皇子協為帝。」
paragraphs.prose: Just as he was hesitating, Pan Yin arrived and said, "The Emperor has died. At this moment Jian Shuo and the Ten Permanent Attendants are conspiring to keep the death secret, and have forged an edict summoning the Royal Uncle He Jin into the palace, intending to cut off all later peril and to install Prince Xie as the new Emperor."
paragraphs.rhyme:
While yet [He Jin](char-he-jin) in doubt was making stay,
Pan Yin came in, his news without delay:
"The king hath died this hour: [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) and Ten
Conspire to keep the death conceal'd from men;
A forg'd decree they frame, in royal name,
To call you, Lord, before their hidden game;
To cut off future trouble, they would bring
[Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) to mount the throne and reign as king."

paragraphs.original: 說未了，使命至，宣進速入，以定後事。操曰：「今日之計，先宜正君位，然後圖賊。」進曰：「誰敢與吾正君討賊？」一人挺身出曰：「願借精兵五千，斬關入內，冊立新君，盡誅閹豎，掃清朝廷，以安天下！」進視之，乃司徒袁逢之子，袁隗之姪：名紹，字本初，見為司隸校尉。何進大喜，遂點御林軍五千。紹全身披掛。何進引何顒、荀攸、鄭泰等大臣三十餘員，相繼而入，就靈帝柩前，扶立太子辯即皇帝位。
paragraphs.prose: Before the words were finished, an envoy arrived, summoning He Jin to enter the palace at once, to settle the affairs of succession. Cao Cao said, "Today's plan is, first, to set the rightful sovereign upon the throne; afterward, to deal with the conspirators." He Jin said, "Who dares to come with me to set up the rightful king and strike down the bandits?" One man stepped forth, saying, "I beg the loan of five thousand picked troops; I will smash through the gates and enter the palace, install the new sovereign, put all the eunuchs to death, sweep the court clean, and bring peace to the realm!" He Jin looked: it was the son of the Minister of the Masses Yuan Feng, and the nephew of Yuan Wei: Shao by name, with the courtesy name Benchu, then serving as Director of Retainers. He Jin was greatly pleased, and at once mustered five thousand of the imperial guard. Shao armed himself fully. He Jin led He Yong, Xun You, Zheng Tai, and other great ministers, more than thirty in all, who entered together, and before Emperor Ling's coffin set up the Crown Prince Bian to ascend the imperial throne.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Ere yet the words were done, a herald near
Brought royal summons; bade [He Jin](char-he-jin) appear,
To settle there the after-throne's affair.
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) said: "First, the rightful heir declare;
Then, after, plot to crush the rebel band."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) then said: "Who dares with sword in hand
To set the rightful heir, and crush the foe?"
A man stepp'd forth: "Five thousand troops bestow,
And I shall break the gates, install the king;
The eunuchs all I'll slay, and silence bring;
Sweep clean the court, and to the realm restore
Such peace as Han's wide realm hath known before."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) then mark'd him: Yuan Feng's son was there,
Yuan Wei's nephew, bold with martial air;
Director of Retainers, [Shao](char-yuan-shao) was known,
Who armed himself, his loyal purpose shown.
With He Yong, Xun You, Zheng Tai, in array,
And thirty more of court, they march'd straightway,
Before [Ling](char-emperor-ling)'s coffin, gathered in array,
They raised [Prince Bian](char-prince-bian) to imperial sway.

paragraphs.original: 百官呼拜已畢，袁紹入宮收蹇碩。碩慌走入御花園花陰下為中常侍郭勝所殺。碩所領禁軍，盡皆投順。紹謂何進曰：「中官結黨。今日可乘勢盡誅之。」張讓等知事急，慌入告何后曰：「始初設謀陷害大將軍者，止蹇碩一人，並不干臣等事。今大將軍聽袁紹之言，欲盡誅臣等，乞娘娘憐憫！」何太后曰：「汝等勿憂，我當保汝。」傳旨宣何進入。太后密謂曰：「我與汝出身寒微，非張讓等，焉能享此富貴？今蹇碩不仁，既已伏誅，汝何信人言，欲盡誅宦官耶？」
paragraphs.prose: After all the officials had paid their homage, Yuan Shao entered the palace to apprehend Jian Shuo. Shuo, in panic, fled into the imperial flower garden, where, beneath the shade of the blossoms, he was killed by the Permanent Attendant Guo Sheng. The forbidden troops which Shuo had commanded all turned and submitted. Yuan Shao said to He Jin, "The court eunuchs have formed a faction. This day we may take advantage, and put them all to death." Zhang Rang and the others, knowing the matter was urgent, hurried in to Empress Dowager He and pleaded, "He who first laid the plot to harm the Grand General was Jian Shuo alone, and had nothing to do with us, Your Majesty's servants. Now the Grand General hearkens to the words of Yuan Shao and would put us all to death — we beg Your Majesty's mercy!" The Empress Dowager He said, "Have no fear; I shall protect you." She sent down a summons, calling He Jin into the palace. The Empress Dowager privately said to him, "You and I rose from a low and humble origin; without Zhang Rang and the rest, how could we have come to enjoy such wealth and honor? Now Jian Shuo, the cruel one, has already been put to death. Why do you give ear to others' words, and wish to put all the eunuchs to death?"
paragraphs.rhyme:
Their homage done, [Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao), armed for fight,
Enter'd the palace, seeking [Shuo](char-jian-shuo) outright.
[Shuo](char-jian-shuo) fled in panic to the garden's bowers,
Where [Guo Sheng](char-guo-sheng) struck him dead beneath the flowers.
The guards he led at once their arms laid by;
And [Shao](char-yuan-shao) to [He Jin](char-he-jin) spake with eager eye:
"The eunuch faction in this hour we may
Strike down — not one shall make escape this day."
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and rest, alarm'd, before the queen
Bow'd low, and cried: "[Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo)'s was all the scheme;
We had no part — yet [Shao](char-yuan-shao) would slay us all!
Have mercy, Lady, ere our houses fall!"
The queen reply'd: "Have fear of nought today:
I'll keep your lives, and turn the harm away."
She call'd [He Jin](char-he-jin) in private to her side,
And spoke these words when none were there beside:
"Both thou and I from humble blood arose;
But for [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), who would our rise suppose?
How else could wealth and honor crown our state?
Now [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo)'s crime hath met its proper fate.
Why trust men's words, and seek in angry mood
To spill the eunuchs' unoffending blood?"

paragraphs.original: 何進聽罷，出謂眾官曰：「蹇碩設謀害我，可族滅其家。其餘不必妄加殘害。」袁紹曰：「若不斬草除根，必為喪身之本。」進曰：「吾意已決，汝勿多言。」眾官皆退。
paragraphs.prose: He Jin, hearing this through, came forth and said to the assembled officials, "Jian Shuo plotted to kill me; for that, his clan may be put to extermination. As for the rest, there is no need to harm them in vain." Yuan Shao said, "If you do not cut the grass at the root, this will be the seed of your own destruction." He Jin said, "My mind is set; speak no more." The officials all withdrew.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[He Jin](char-he-jin), the queen's persuasion fully heard,
Came forth before the lords, and gave his word:
"[Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) alone the plot 'gainst me design'd,
His clan be slain; the rest no harm shall find."
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) reply'd: "Unless the roots be cleft,
This seed shall grow, and leave our bodies reft."
"My mind is set," [He Jin](char-he-jin) in answer said;
"Speak thou no more — return now to thy stead."

paragraphs.original: 次日，太后命何進參錄尚書事，其餘皆封官職。董太后宣張讓等入宮商議曰：「何進之妹，始初我抬舉他。今日他孩兒即皇帝位，內外臣僚，皆其心腹：威權太重，我將如何？」讓奏曰：「娘娘可臨朝，垂簾聽政；封皇子協為王；加國舅董重大官，掌握軍權；重用臣等：大事可圖矣。」
paragraphs.prose: The next day, the Empress Dowager He commanded that He Jin be appointed to administer the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat, and the others were all granted office and rank. The Empress Dowager Dong summoned Zhang Rang and the rest into the palace to take counsel, saying, "He Jin's sister — at the beginning it was I who raised her up. Today her son sits upon the throne, and the ministers within the court and without are all his trusted men. His power is too heavy; what shall I do?" Rang memorialized, "Your Majesty may yourself attend court, listening to government from behind the curtain; enfeoff Prince Xie as Prince; promote the Royal Uncle Dong Zhong to a great office, with command of the armies; rely on us, your servants — and the great matter may be planned."

paragraphs.original: 董太后大喜。次日設朝，董太后降旨，封皇子協為陳留王，董重為驃騎將軍，張讓等共預朝政。何太后見董太后專權，於宮中設一宴，請董太后赴席。酒至半酣，何太后起身捧盃再拜曰：「我等皆婦人也，參預朝政，非其所宜。昔呂后因握重權，宗族千口皆被戮。今我等宜深居九重；朝廷大事，任大臣元老自行商議，此國家之幸也。願垂聽焉。」董太后大怒曰：「汝鴆死王美人，設心嫉妒。今倚汝子為君，與汝兄何進之勢，輒敢亂言！吾敕驃騎斷汝兄首，如反掌耳！」何后亦怒曰：「吾以好言相勸，何反怒耶？」董后曰：「汝家屠沽小輩，有何見識！」
paragraphs.prose: The Empress Dowager Dong was greatly pleased. The next day a court was held, and the Empress Dowager Dong issued an edict making Prince Xie the Prince of Chenliu, and Dong Zhong General of Agile Cavalry; and Zhang Rang and his fellows shared in the affairs of the court. The Empress Dowager He, seeing that the Empress Dowager Dong had seized authority for herself, set out a feast in the palace and invited the Empress Dowager Dong to it. When the wine had reached its half-mellow stage, the Empress Dowager He rose and held up a cup, bowed twice, and said, "We are all women: to take part in the affairs of court is not what is fitting for us. In days past Empress Lü, because she grasped heavy power, saw her clan of a thousand mouths all slaughtered. Today we should keep ourselves deep within the nine-fold palace; let the great matters of court be discussed and decided by the great ministers and elders themselves — this is the fortune of the state. Pray, listen and lend your ear to this." The Empress Dowager Dong was greatly enraged, and said, "You poisoned the Lady Wang, in jealous heart! Now, leaning on your son the king and on the power of your brother He Jin, you dare speak so wildly! I shall command the General of Agile Cavalry to cut off your brother's head — as easy as turning my hand!" The Empress Dowager He also was enraged, and said, "I urged you with kind words; why answer with anger?" The Empress Dowager Dong said, "Your butcher-and-wine-seller's brood — what understanding have you?"
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong), hugely glad, the morrow held a court:
[Prince Xie](char-prince-xie) made Prince of Chenliu, by her sort;
And [Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong) rais'd to Agile General's stand;
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and his shar'd in the realm's command.
The [Empress He](char-empress-he), who saw [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) claim it all,
A banquet spread within the palace-hall;
She bade the Dowager attend her cheer,
And when the wine was half, the moment near,
She rose, twice bow'd, and held a cup in air,
And spake at length, with calm and humble care:
"We women, both — to meddle in affairs
Of state becomes us ill. Recall the fate
Of Empress Lü, who bore such heavy weight;
Beheld her thousand kin in slaughter pain'd.
By that strict warning, madam, be we stay'd;
Retire we deep within the palace shade,
And leave to elders of the court the deeds
Of state — and thus the realm in fortune speeds."
Then [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong), in fury, made her answer start:
"Thou poison'dst Lady Wang in jealous heart!
Now leaning on thy son and brother's might,
Thou darest speak thus rashly in our sight!
I'll bid the Agile General, at my call,
Strike off thy brother's head within the hall!"
The [Empress He](char-empress-he), in turn, took fire and said:
"I gave good counsel — wherefore wrath, instead?"
[Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) then reply'd: "Thou butcher-merchant's clan —
What understanding hath the common man?"

paragraphs.original: 兩宮互相爭競，張讓等各勸歸宮。何后連夜召何進入宮，告以前事。何進出，召三公共議：來早設朝，使廷臣奏董太后原係藩妃，不宜久居宮中，合仍遷於河間安置，限日下即出國門。一面遣人起送董后；一面點禁軍圍驃騎將軍董重府宅，追索印綬。董重知事急，自刎於後堂。家人舉哀，軍士方散。張讓、段珪見董后一枝已廢，遂皆以金珠玩好結搆何進弟何曲并其母舞陽君，令早晚入何太后處，善言遮蔽：因此十常侍又得近幸。
paragraphs.prose: The two palaces contended with each other; Zhang Rang and his fellows each persuaded their patroness to return to her own palace. The Empress Dowager He, that very night, summoned He Jin into the palace and told him all that had passed. He Jin went out and called the Three Ducal Ministers to deliberate: at the next morning's audience, the court ministers were to memorialize that the Empress Dowager Dong, originally being the wife of a feudal-lord, was not fit to dwell long within the palace, and should accordingly be removed to Hejian to be settled there, and should depart from the gates of the realm at once. On one side they dispatched men to escort the Empress Dowager Dong away; on the other, they mustered the imperial guards to surround the residence of the General of Agile Cavalry Dong Zhong, and demanded the surrender of his seal-cord. Dong Zhong, knowing the matter was urgent, cut his own throat in the rear hall. His family raised the lamentations of mourning, and the soldiers thereupon dispersed. Zhang Rang and Duan Gui, seeing that the Empress Dowager Dong's branch had already been cut off, then with gold and pearls and rare playthings sought ties with He Jin's brother He Miao and his mother Lady Wuyang, sending them at all hours into the Empress Dowager He's apartments to speak well of the eunuchs and shield them. By this means the Ten Permanent Attendants again gained the imperial favor.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The two factions strove in bitter coil;
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and his bade each withdraw from broil.
That night the [Empress He](char-empress-he) call'd to her side
[He Jin](char-he-jin), and told what words had passed inside.
[He Jin](char-he-jin) went forth, and call'd the [Three](misc-three-ducal-ministers) to plan,
To frame the morrow's measure in their span.
At dawn the court address'd the throne with prayer:
"[Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong), once a feudal-lord's wife, may not bear
Within the palace dwell — let her be sent
To Hejian, ere the day's brief course be spent."
On one side, men were sent to bear her hence;
On other, troops surround [Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong)'s defense,
And there demanded his commission's seal.
[Dong Zhong](char-dong-zhong), who saw the danger at his heel,
Cut his own throat, and in the rear hall died.
His kin wail'd loud; the soldiers stood aside.
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), [Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), who saw [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong)'s branch was done,
With gold and pearls and toys made bond, each one,
With [He Miao](char-he-miao), brother to the General near,
And Lady Wuyang, [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s mother dear:
They bid the pair, by day and night, attend
The [Empress He](char-empress-he), and for the Ten extend
Defense and praise — and through this quiet art,
The Ten Attendants gain'd the queen's fond heart.

paragraphs.original: 六月，何進暗使人酖殺董后於河間驛庭，舉柩回京，葬於文陵。進託病不出，司隸校尉袁紹入見進曰：「張讓、段珪等流言於外，言公酖殺董后，欲謀大事。乘此時不誅閹宦，後必為大禍。昔竇武欲誅內豎，機謀不密，反受其殃。今公兄弟部曲將吏，皆英俊之士；若使盡力，事在掌握。此天贊之時，不可失也。」進曰：「且容商議。」左右密報張讓﹔讓等轉告何苗，又多送賄賂。苗入奏何后云：「大將軍輔佐新君，不行仁慈，專務殺伐。今無瑞又欲殺十常侍，此取亂之道也。」后納其言。
paragraphs.prose: In the sixth month, He Jin secretly sent men to poison Empress Dowager Dong at the post-station courtyard of Hejian; her coffin was borne back to the capital and buried at Wenling. He Jin pleaded sickness and did not go forth. The Director of Retainers Yuan Shao came in to see He Jin and said, "Zhang Rang, Duan Gui and the rest are spreading abroad the rumor that My Lord poisoned the Dowager Dong and means now to compass a great design. To take this moment and not put the eunuchs to death will surely bring great disaster afterwards. In old days, Dou Wu wished to put the inner ministers to death; his plan was not closely kept, and he suffered the harm in turn. Now your brother's officers and captains under his command are all men of brilliance and worth; if they be set to their full strength, the matter is in your grasp. This is a moment when Heaven favors you, and not to be let slip." He Jin said, "Let it be considered for a while." His attendants secretly carried report to Zhang Rang; Rang and the rest in turn passed word to He Miao, and sent yet more bribes. Miao went in and memorialized to Empress He, saying, "The Grand General assists the new sovereign; he does not act in benevolence and mercy, but devotes himself wholly to slaughter. Now, without good cause, he would put the Ten Permanent Attendants to death — this is the way to bring on disorder." The Empress accepted his words.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In sixth month, [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s hand, by stealth, was sent
To poison [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong) within the post-house tent;
Her coffin home was brought, with mourning train,
And buried at the Wenling's level plain.
[He Jin](char-he-jin), by pretext of an illness feign'd,
Withdrew, and from the public ways refrain'd.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) came in to [He Jin](char-he-jin), drawing near,
And spake to him with countenance severe:
"[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) and his abroad now whisper rife
That thou hast poison'd [Dong](char-empress-dowager-dong), and seek'st more strife,
That at the throne thou'st set thy secret eye.
This is the moment: thou must not deny
Their slaughter; if thou let'st this hour go past,
Calamity shall fall on us at last.
Dou Wu of old such counsel held in mind:
To slay the inner servants — but, behind
His thought, the secret leak'd, and he was slain.
Thy brothers' captains all are heroes plain;
Set them to work — and triumph lies in hand;
This Heaven-favor'd hour, take thou thy stand!"
[He Jin](char-he-jin) reply'd: "Let me consider on."
His men, in secret, told the Ten anon.
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) told [Miao](char-he-miao), with bribes anew bestow'd;
[Miao](char-he-miao) to the [Empress](char-empress-he) went, where she abode,
And said: "The General, with no merc'ful hand,
Pursues but slaughter, by his stern command.
Without good cause he'd slay the Ten — and so
Bring chaos in. Beware this dreadful blow!"
The [Empress](char-empress-he) heeded; thus she gave consent
To stay [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s design — the Ten content.

paragraphs.original: 少頃，何進入白后，欲誅中涓。何后曰：「中官統領禁省，漢家故事。先帝新棄天下，爾欲誅殺舊臣，非重宗廟也。」進本是沒決斷之人，聽太后言，唯唯而出。袁紹迎問曰：「大事若何？」進曰：「太后不允，如之奈何？」紹曰：「可召四方英雄人士，勒兵來京，盡誅閹豎。此時事急，不容太后不從。」進曰：「此計大妙！」便發檄至各鎮，召赴京師。
paragraphs.prose: A little while later, He Jin entered and told the Empress that he wished to put the eunuchs to death. Empress He said, "The court eunuchs head the imperial guard within the palace — this is the old custom of the Han house. The late Emperor has just departed from the world; you would kill these old ministers — this is no honoring of the ancestral temple." He Jin was by nature an undecisive man; hearing the Empress's words, he murmured assent and withdrew. Yuan Shao met him and asked, "How does the great matter stand?" He Jin said, "The Empress will not consent; what is to be done?" Shao said, "Summon the brave men of the four quarters, with their forces, to come up to the capital; together they shall put all the eunuchs to death. The matter is urgent, and the Empress cannot but consent." He Jin said, "An excellent plan!" — and at once dispatched proclamations to each garrison, calling them up to the capital.
paragraphs.rhyme:
A little after, [He Jin](char-he-jin) enter'd in
And told the queen his purpose; 'gainst the kin
Of eunuch-pow'r he'd draw his vengeful blade.
She answer'd him: "By Han's old custom laid,
The eunuchs lead the inner guard by right;
The late Emperor hath but passed from sight;
Wouldst thou now slay old servants of the line,
And fail in reverence to the ancestral shrine?"
[He Jin](char-he-jin), by nature undecided, slack,
Heard out the queen, and yielding, drew aback.
[Yuan Shao](char-yuan-shao) came forth: "How stands the great affair?"
[He Jin](char-he-jin) reply'd: "The queen will not declare
Her yielding — what must now be undertook?"
Said [Shao](char-yuan-shao): "Call up the heroes of the brook
And mountain — bring their armies hither all;
At one swift stroke, the eunuchs shall not call
For mercy. In this hour the queen must bend."
[He Jin](char-he-jin): "A wondrous plan; I shall attend!"
And forth he sent the summons broad and wide,
Calling each garrison unto his side.

paragraphs.original: 主簿陳琳曰：「不可！俗云：『掩目而捕燕雀』，是自欺也。微物尚不可欺以得志，況國家大事乎？今將軍仗皇威，掌兵要，龍驤虎步，高下在心：若欲誅宦官，如鼓洪爐燎毛髮耳。但當速發，行權立斷，則天人順之﹔卻反外檄大臣，臨犯京闕，英雄聚會，各懷一心：所謂倒持干戈，授人以柄，功必一成，反生亂矣。」何進笑曰：「此懦夫之見也！」傍邊一人鼓掌大笑曰：「此事易如反掌，何必多議！」視之，乃曹操也。正是：欲除君側宵人亂，須聽朝中智士謀。不知曹操說出甚話來，且聽下文分解。
paragraphs.prose: The Chief Recorder Chen Lin said, "It cannot be! The proverb says, 'covering one's eyes to catch the swallow,' — that is to deceive oneself. Small creatures cannot be deceived to one's purpose, and how much less the great affairs of the state? Now Your Lordship leans on the imperial authority and holds command of the troops; you stride as a dragon and stalk as a tiger, with the high and the low at your will. If you would put the eunuchs to death, it is like fanning a great furnace to scorch hair. Only act swiftly, in measure and decision, and Heaven and men will follow you. But to summon great ministers from without, that they should march upon the capital — when heroes gather, each will hold a heart of his own. This is what is called 'reversing the spear, and giving the handle into another's grasp.' The deed cannot succeed; on the contrary, it will breed disorder." He Jin laughed: "This is the view of a coward!" Beside him a man clapped his hands and laughed aloud, saying, "This matter is as easy as turning over the hand — what need of so much discussion?" Looking, it was Cao Cao. So it is said: "Would you root out the schemers beside the ruler? — listen to the wise counselors of the court." Not knowing what Cao Cao would say, hearken to the next chapter for the unfolding.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Chen Lin, Chief Recorder, rose to make his stand:
"It cannot be! The proverbs of the land
Declare: 'To shut the eyes and catch the bird
Is self-deceit.' All men of sense have heard
That small things foil a self-deceiving heart:
How then the realm's great matters by such art?
Thy lordship, with imperial might endow'd,
And armies in thy grasp, the realm enthrall'd,
At thy command both high and low must bow:
To slay the eunuchs is a slight one now,
As easy as to fan a glowing fire
Whose flame consumes a hair: but firm thy ire,
With speed, decisive — then will heaven and man
Together bear thee forward in thy plan.
But shouldst thou call from far the captains' force,
With heroes flocking, each upon his course,
'Tis spear revers'd, the haft to others thrown;
Thy deed must fail; instead, dark chaos sown."
[He Jin](char-he-jin) laugh'd loud: "A coward's word, no more!"
Beside him, one with claps the silence tore:
"This deed is light as turning of the hand,
Why all this counsel? Let the matter stand!"
They look'd: 'twas [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao). Now indeed it ran:
Wouldst purge the throne of schemers? Heed the plan
That court's wise scholars frame, and act anon.
What [Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) spake, the next chapter makes known.
